rawEventDetails: Speaker Yulai Zhao Details Event Description This dissertation investigates the alignment and theoretical foundations of generative AI through reinforcement learning (RL).We bridge the gap between rigorous mathematical guarantees and practical alignment across two primary parts. In Part I (Alignment of Generative Systems), we first expose systematic vulnerability in the LLM-as-a-Judge framework, identifying “master keys”: non-informative adversarial patterns that consistently trigger high false-positive rates, and we propose a robust reward model to mitigate these exploits. Moreover, we enhance diffusion models by introducing a sample-efficient online fine-tuning algorithm that utilizes optimistic exploration. Furthermore, we develop a direct back-propagation framework that enables adding precise, conditional control to diffusion models with superior sample efficiency. In Part II (Reinforcement Learning Theory), we establish foundational guarantees for complex environments. We provide the first proof that local policy optimization achieves global optimality in cooperative multi-agent RL with function approximation. Finally, we develop the first provably efficient algorithm for CVaR (Conditional Value-at-Risk) RL in low-rank MDPs. title: Towards Physics-Guided Wireless Communication and Sensing Above 100 GHz
series: Final Public Oral Examinations,Final Public Orals
content: The sub-Terahertz (sub-THz) bands - frequencies above 100 GHz and up to 1 THz - are rapidly emerging as one of the accepted paradigms for future wireless networks. In principle, these frequencies can provide ultra-fast data transmission due to their large amount of available bandwidth. Nonetheless, several fundamental challenges stand in the way of their adoption. Instead of merely scaling the existing wireless system architecture, my thesis investigates how to leverage the physics of sub-THz signals to overcome these hurdles.
rawEventDetails: Speaker Atsutse Kludze Details Event Description The sub-Terahertz (sub-THz) bands - frequencies above 100 GHz and up to 1 THz - are rapidly emerging as one of the accepted paradigms for future wireless networks. In principle, these frequencies can provide ultra-fast data transmission due to their large amount of available bandwidth. Nonetheless, several fundamental challenges stand in the way of their adoption. Instead of merely scaling the existing wireless system architecture, my thesis investigates how to leverage the physics of sub-THz signals to overcome these hurdles. One of the biggest obstacles is power consumption, since generating and amplifying signals above 100 GHz requires power-hungry circuitry. This issue is compounded by severe path loss, which demands highly directional links created by large antenna arrays. To address this, my thesis introduces LeakyScatter, a new passive architecture that enables wideband backscattering above 100 GHz. By exploiting leaky-wave antenna physics, LeakyScatter establishes retro-directive links without active components or power consumption. Power alone, however, does not determine scalability: sub-THz networks also demand devices that can be manufactured over large areas at low cost. To this end, I introduce a new class of broadband, electronically reconfigurable sub-THz metasurfaces whose active element is an organic electrochemical modulator. By electrochemically doping and de-doping large-area patterned organic films, these devices dynamically control the polarization, spectral response, and direction of sub-THz wavefronts at milliwatt-scale power, using fabrication processes compatible with large-area organic electronics. Next, given the emergence of high-frequency devices with electronically large aperture sizes, wireless users may fall into the near-field of an access point, where traditional far-field assumptions break down. I develop analytical and simulation frameworks to evaluate near-field beamforming performance and demonstrate how multiple coordinated arrays can overcome existing range and focusing limitations. Lastly, I explore how sub-THz signals can address pressing real-world challenges far beyond traditional wireless networking, enabling unprecedented sensing functionalities: non-coherent 3D localization from a single broadband transmission, and non-destructive fruit-quality monitoring that targets large-scale food waste where existing methods are invasive or economically impractical. Collectively, these efforts contribute foundational physical-layer architectures and device technologies for next-generation wireless networks. Adviser: Yasaman Ghasempour
summaryRaw: Towards Physics-Guided Wireless Communication and Sensing Above 100 GHz

title: Deep Learning Across the Communication Stack: From Channel Coding to Task-Aware Transmission
series: Final Public Oral Examinations,Final Public Orals
content: Modern communication systems operate remarkably close to fundamental limits, but their design has historically relied on carefully engineered mathematical structure. In channel coding, for example, learning must generalize across an exponentially large message space that no practical training set can cover.This dissertation argues that classical
rawEventDetails: Speaker Shibara Ashwin Hebbar Details Event Description Modern communication systems operate remarkably close to fundamental limits, but their design has historically relied on carefully engineered mathematical structure. Deep learning offers a complementary capability: learning representations and decision rules directly from data. Bringing this capability to communication, however, is difficult. In channel coding, for example, learning must generalize across an exponentially large message space that no practical training set can cover. This dissertation argues that classical structure and learned optimization play complementary roles in communication system design. It develops a framework of neural augmentation, in which learned components are embedded within classical systems. The classical design organizes computation, guides training, and constrains what learning may change, while learning is concentrated on the operation or representation that limits performance. We develop this principle at progressively deeper levels of the communication stack. TinyTurbo retains the Turbo decoding algorithm and learns a low-dimensional correction to the exchanged soft information, recovering much of the loss introduced by the max-log-MAP approximation. CRISP preserves the sequential structure of Polar and PAC decoding, but learns the conditional decision rules using a curriculum derived from nested subcodes, approaching the reliability of stronger classical decoders without list search or backtracking. DeepPolar goes further by learning the code itself together with a matched decoder. It replaces fixed binary Polar kernels with learned nonlinear transformations while retaining the recursive construction and successive decoding structure needed for scalability. The resulting codes improve reliability over classical Polar and Reed–Muller codes under successive-cancellation decoding. DeepOFDM extends neural augmentation from coding to modulation, replacing independent symbol-wise mappings with context-dependent neural modulation whose gains are largest under high mobility and sparse or absent pilots. Finally, we move iii beyond bit-level fidelity to task-aware source coding for vision-language receivers. Using the question as side information, FoCAL preserves task-relevant image detail and reduces rate by 28–57% at matched downstream performance while keeping the receiver frozen. A complementary codec adaptation transfers across multiple receivers without additional retraining. Across these systems, a consistent picture emerges: classical structure provides the architectural and training biases that make learning tractable, while learning improves the approximations and representations that classical design leaves suboptimal. Adviser: Pramod Viswanath
summaryRaw: Deep Learning Across the Communication Stack: From Channel Coding to Task-Aware Transmission

title: Charge Transfer States and Polarons in Organic Donor-Acceptor Diodes: Generation, Recombination, and Their Interplay
series: Final Public Oral Examinations,Final Public Orals
content: Organic solar cells and organic photodetectors combine mechanical flexibility, solution processability, and spectral tunability from the visible to the near infrared, yet their performance remains limited by large voltage losses and parasitic dark currents compared with inorganic counterparts. In donor–acceptor (D–A) heterojunction diodes, nonradiative recombination via charge transfer (CT) states broadened by energetic disorder is a key origin of voltage loss, but reliable approaches for quantifying CT state disorder are not yet
rawEventDetails: Speaker Manting Gui Details Event Description Organic solar cells and organic photodetectors combine mechanical flexibility, solution processability, and spectral tunability from the visible to the near infrared, yet their performance remains limited by large voltage losses and parasitic dark currents compared with inorganic counterparts. In donor–acceptor (D–A) heterojunction diodes, nonradiative recombination via charge transfer (CT) states broadened by energetic disorder is a key origin of voltage loss, but reliable approaches for quantifying CT state disorder are not yet well-recognized in the community. In parallel, intrinsic dark current generation is increasingly attributed to deep trap states, while its microscopic origin and the deviations from ideal diode behavior are still not fully clarified. This thesis investigates new nonradiative recombination and dark current generation pathways using a combination of steady state and spectroscopic techniques to characterize CT states, associated energy loss, and the thermal dependence of dark current and charge transport. Studies on a series of amorphous and crystalline organic diodes, and inorganic-organic hybrid diodes show that hole polarons play a central role in organic systems by introducing additional nonradiative energy loss channels and inducing extra dark current generation, detrimental for both photovoltaic and photodetector operation. A specific mechanism is identified in which NIR hole polarons act as antennas in D–A blends, facilitating thermal excitation of CT states and inherently driving dark current. The activation energy of the reverse saturation dark current is found to track the activation energy of hole polaron transport, highlighting polaron dynamics as a key control parameter. Overall, device behavior is rationalized as a coupled CT–polaron problem: under illumination, CT recombination governed by the energy gap law, together with CT-polaron spectral overlap, enhances voltage loss and fundamentally limits photocurrent; whereas in the dark, the spectral overlap of blackbody radiation with CT and polaron absorption sets an effective generation prefactor for the dark current. Finally, inorganic–organic hybrid diodes, exemplified by CuSCN/organic acceptor heterojunctions, exhibit substantially reduced dark currents relative to fully organic devices, indicating their potential for high detectivity near infrared photodetectors. Adviser: Barry Rand
summaryRaw: Charge Transfer States and Polarons in Organic Donor-Acceptor Diodes: Generation, Recombination, and Their Interplay

title: Securing Domain Validation Against Network Attacks: Deployable Defenses for the Web PKI
series: Final Public Oral Examinations,Final Public Orals
content: HTTPS underpins secure communication on the Web, but its trust is bootstrapped through domain control validation (DV) : a challenge-response protocol through which Certificate Authorities (CAs) verify the requester' s control of a domain name. DV relies on unauthenticated protocols (including BGP, DNS, and HTTP), and is therefore vulnerable to network-level attacks that can enable fraudulent certificate issuance. rawEventDetails: Speaker Grace Cimaszewski Details Event Description HTTPS underpins secure communication on the Web, but its trust is bootstrapped through domain control validation (DV) : a challenge-response protocol through which Certificate Authorities (CAs) verify the requester' s control of a domain name. DV relies on unauthenticated protocols (including BGP, DNS, and HTTP), and is therefore vulnerable to network-level attacks that can enable fraudulent certificate issuance. This thesis hardens DV against network attacks through three deployable defenses spanning ecosystem-wide protection and opt-in cryptographic guarantees, and translates them into real-world standards and deployment. First, we quantify and strengthen multi-perspective issuance corroboration (MPIC). Using a custom full-graph DNS resolver, we present the first Internet-scale measurement of DV' s complete attack surface, covering 1. 1 M domains and over 31 billion DNS queries. Bringing DNS into scope drops single-perspective resilience from 86% to 38%; strategic placement of five diverse vantage points with a unanimous quorum policy restores it to 97%. These findings shaped CA/ Browser Forum Ballot SC-067v3, which standardized the core MPIC framework evaluated here and mandated it for server certificate issuance starting September 2025. MPIC has thus protected over 1. 5 billion certificates to date. Second, we present cryptographically-secure DV ("crypto-DV"), a framework providing cryptographic issuance guarantees for opt-in domains. Using DNSSEC trust roots, CAs boot-strap secure channels with domain owners and validate DV challenges with cryptographic integrity. A fail-closed CAA policy enforces this protection under partial deployment: non-implementing CAs must refuse issuance. Its deployment prerequisite, DNSSEC validation by CAs, was mandated by CA/ Browser Forum Ballot SC-085 v2 effective March 2026, and the design informed an IETF working-group draft. Third, we propose secure channel DNS, a scalable alternative to DNSSEC' s stalled per-zone adoption that secures resolver-nameserver communications via encrypted channels. Measuring ~449M domains from Certificate Transparency logs, we find that eight providers host authoritative DNS for 47.7% of measured domains, suggesting that deployment at a few operators could protect resolution for much of the Web. We analyze how SVCB records can support this abstraction and contribute an open-source implementation in Hickory DNS for deployment at Let' a Encrypt. Together, these results show a deployable path for authenticated DNS beyond DNSSEC. Adviser: Prateek Mittal
summaryRaw: Securing Domain Validation Against Network Attacks: Deployable Defenses for the Web PKI

title: Beyond the Monomer: Designing Sequence, Patterns, Composition, and Architecture in Macromolecules
content: Polymers are essential to a wide range of technologies, yet designing them with targeted structural and functional properties remains a grand challenge. Moreover, the products and technology only exploit a fraction of the prospective design space availed by macromolecules. A major opportunity lies in applying machine learning to help navigate the vast combinatorial design space—spanning sequence, composition, architecture, morphology, processing, and more—to discover new formulations or replace existing ones with more sustainable alternatives. However, this complexity, combined with data
rawEventDetails: Speaker Michael Webb Affiliation Princeton University Details Event Description Polymers are essential to a wide range of technologies, yet designing them with targeted structural and functional properties remains a grand challenge. Moreover, the products and technology only exploit a fraction of the prospective design space availed by macromolecules. A major opportunity lies in applying machine learning to help navigate the vast combinatorial design space—spanning sequence, composition, architecture, morphology, processing, and more—to discover new formulations or replace existing ones with more sustainable alternatives. However, this complexity, combined with data scarcity and characterization challenges, limits the effectiveness of purely rational design and/or high-throughput screening. In this talk, I will describe some of our recent efforts to integrate molecular simulation, machine learning, and theory to map and navigate structure–function relationships in chemically and topologically diverse polymeric materials. I will describe strategies that we have employed across a range of applications to overcome data limitations in polymer science by developing physics-informed (or guided) models as well as other algorithmic innovations. Specific examples of our approach will be drawn from the characterization of single-chain nanoparticle morphologies, the design of enzyme-stabilizing copolymers, and the formulation of architecturally complex polymer additives that tune solution rheology. These examples will showcase utility, limitations, and opportunities for data-driven approaches in modern-day science and how coupling them with (or using them to develop) physical insight can accelerate innovation and deepen materials understanding.
summaryRaw: Beyond the Monomer: Designing Sequence, Patterns, Composition, and Architecture in Macromolecules

title: From Closed-Loop Systems to Closed-Loop Design: Full-Stack Co-Design for the AI Era
content: Abstract: Computing systems are becoming increasingly closed loop. A robot continuously senses, computes, and acts in the physical world; more broadly, emerging AI applications interact dynamically with users, tools, and environments. Yet the way we design these systems remains largely open loop: models, software, hardware architectures, and implementations are developed in separate stages, with slow and incomplete feedback across layers. As a result, improvements in isolated metrics such as kernel latency, energy, or hardware utilization do
rawEventDetails: Speaker Yakun Sophia Shao Affiliation University of California, Berkeley Details Event Description Abstract: Computing systems are becoming increasingly closed loop. A robot continuously senses, computes, and acts in the physical world; more broadly, emerging AI applications interact dynamically with users, tools, and environments. Yet the way we design these systems remains largely open loop: models, software, hardware architectures, and implementations are developed in separate stages, with slow and incomplete feedback across layers. As a result, improvements in isolated metrics such as kernel latency, energy, or hardware utilization do not necessarily translate into better end-to-end behavior. In this talk, I will argue that closing this gap requires rethinking both what we design and how we design it. The full computing stack should be treated as a connected, executable design space in which application goals, software, architecture, and implementation continuously inform one another. I will trace our efforts to close this loop: first by making cross-layer consequences observable in end-to-end applications, then by co-designing heterogeneous hardware and software around system-level requirements, and ultimately by using AI to navigate and accelerate the design process itself. I will conclude with a vision for using AI not simply to generate code or implementations, but to participate in system and architecture design itself. By making design choices, constraints, and feedback explicit and machine-operable, we can move toward a closed-loop methodology that connects application goals to deployable systems, from mission to silicon. Bio: Professor Yakun Sophia Shao is The Class of 1951 Chair Associate Professor at the Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences department of University of California, Berkeley. Her research interests are in the area of computer architecture, with a special focus on specialized accelerator, heterogeneous architecture, and agile VLSI design methodology. Previously, she was a Senior Research Scientist at NVIDIA Research and received her Ph.D. degree in 2016 from Harvard University. She is a recipient of the 2025 Outstanding Teaching Award in EE, the 2024 Anita Borg Early Career Award, a Sloan Research Fellowship, an NSF CAREER Award, the 2022 IEEE TCCA Young Computer Architect Award, a Google Faculty Rising Stars Award in Systems Research, a Google Research Scholar Award, a Facebook Research Award, an Okawa Foundation Research Grant, and the inaugural Dr. Sudhakar Yalamanchili Award. Her work has been awarded multiple Best Paper Awards and Distinguished Artifact Awards at major hardware conferences. Sponsor Emerging Frontiers in Computer Architecture and Systems

rawEventDetails: Speaker Gina Noh Affiliation The Pennsylvania State University Details Event Description Structure-function relationships for heterogeneous catalysis play a key role in the development of atom-efficient catalysts, reducing the need for energy-intensive separations or catalyst regeneration protocols and enabling new routes to platform chemicals from abundant feedstocks. The Noh research group at Penn State uses multi-scale approaches, spanning from molecular-level detail to mechanistic assessment of catalysts, and combining experiment and theory (density functional theory, DFT) to understand the nature and speciation of active sites, their communication with other functions, and their consequences for catalysis. In this seminar, I will present two vignettes: (1) dry reforming of methane over Ni-CeO 2 materials and (2) ethanol oxidative dehydrogenation to form acetaldehyde over M1-MoVO x catalysts. The role of elementary steps involving oxygen and oxygen-transport reactions in reactivity, selectivity, and stability will be clarified.

title: Driven-Dissipative Dynamics in Fluxonium: Measurement-Induced Transitions and Effective Temperatures
series: Final Public Oral Examinations,Final Public Orals
content: Superconducting qubits are artificial atoms whose properties are shaped through the engineering of nonlinear electrical circuits. Quantum information is encoded by selecting two levels of this multilevel system to form the computational subspace. Thus, standard operations can inadvertently populate states outside this subspace, producing leakage errors. In transmons, for example, increasing the resonator drive during readout can activate multiphoton resonances that induce measurement-induced state transitions (MISTs), transferring
rawEventDetails: Speaker Parth Jatakia Details Event Description Superconducting qubits are artificial atoms whose properties are shaped through the engineering of nonlinear electrical circuits. Quantum information is encoded by selecting two levels of this multilevel system to form the computational subspace. Thus, standard operations can inadvertently populate states outside this subspace, producing leakage errors. In transmons, for example, increasing the resonator drive during readout can activate multiphoton resonances that induce measurement-induced state transitions (MISTs), transferring population to high-lying states and severely reducing measurement fidelity. MISTs therefore constrain attempts to make dispersive readout simultaneously faster and more accurately. Fluxonium pushes this engineering further, suppressing several sources of decoherence within the computational subspace. This produces an unusually rich, strongly anharmonic spectrum in which higher levels can couple more strongly to microwave fields, without the simple nearest-neighbour selection structure of transmons. The first part of this dissertation examines how MISTs arise in fluxonium and what sets their magnitude. Using flux-pulse-assisted measurements, we uncover population transfer that multiphoton resonances alone cannot explain. To explain them, we perform time-dependent open-quantum-system simulations incorporating driven multilevel dynamics and dissipation. The simulations reveal a new decay-assisted pathway for MISTs: the readout drive populates hybridized states involving higher fluxonium levels, while decay redirects population into the excited qubit manifold. We find that the combined action of drive and decay produces an optical-pumping-like transfer that builds up over the measurement pulse. Multiphoton resonances therefore provide pathways for MISTs, while their magnitude depends continuously on the drive protocol and the environment. The second part of this work examines this environment and the processes through which it exchanges energy with the qubit. Existing fluxonium loss models are phenomenological and cannot by themselves pinpoint the microscopic process or material source of dissipation. We therefore measure excitation and relaxation separately, resolving the environment’s ability to supply and absorb energy. Their imbalance defines a transition-specific effective temperature, while flux tunability turns the rates into a spectral probe of the environment. Across frequency and devices, the directed rates reveal substantial variation, underscoring the complexity of the environment governing qubit dissipation. Adviser: Andrew Houck
summaryRaw: Driven-Dissipative Dynamics in Fluxonium: Measurement-Induced Transitions and Effective Temperatures

title: Molecular Mechanisms Underlying Condensed-Phase Phenomena: Insights from Atomistic Simulations
content: The performance of modern materials often depends on achieving a precise balance among multiple, sometimes competing, properties. Design and optimization of such materials require understanding how subtle variations in molecular composition and organization change this balance. However, this relationship is often difficult to predict as macroscopic properties originate from many interactions occurring at length and time scales far smaller than those directly observed. Molecular simulations provide a means to bridge this gap by relating molecular-level behavior to material response. This
rawEventDetails: Speaker Baris Eser Ugur Details Event Description The performance of modern materials often depends on achieving a precise balance among multiple, sometimes competing, properties. Design and optimization of such materials require understanding how subtle variations in molecular composition and organization change this balance. However, this relationship is often difficult to predict as macroscopic properties originate from many interactions occurring at length and time scales far smaller than those directly observed. Molecular simulations provide a means to bridge this gap by relating molecular-level behavior to material response. This dissertation combines physics-based molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and data-driven machine learning techniques to investigate how molecular chemistry governs physical properties across diverse organic condensed-phase systems, particularly molecular liquids and polymeric materials. In the case of molecular liquids, the central challenge is determining how strongly nuclear quantum effects (NQEs) influence thermophysical properties across chemical space. For polymeric materials, the challenge lies in resolving how functional group chemistry, mixture composition, and comonomer sequence underlie distinct physical phenomena in structurally complex systems. The studies presented here address distinct challenges in relating molecular chemistry to macroscopic properties in complex condensed-phase systems. Together, these insights provide molecular-level principles for understanding physical phenomena and help guide the rational design of high-performance materials.

rawEventDetails: Speaker Kevin Dorfman Affiliation University of Minnesota Details Event Description This presentation will explore our recent computational research self-assembled network phases in block copolymers, which can serve as templates for creating metallic metamaterials. In the first part of the presentation, I will describe routes to produce single-gyroid phases, chiral network with three-fold connectors. While single gyroid is metastable in simple AB diblock copolymers, blends of linear diblock polymers and neat melts of nonlinear copolymer architectures expose stability windows for alternating gyroid and single gyroid, respectively, in experimentally accessible systems. The second part of the presentation will discuss a new principle, known as boundary frustration, that guides termination plane selection between two non-preferential surfaces. Finally, I will describe a new approach known as “generative SCFT” that leverages generative adversarial networks to learn from self-consistent field theory (SCFT) solution trajectories to propose new initial guesses for subsequent SCFT calculations. This approach not only identified all known block polymer network phases but also uncovered a vast library of candidate network phases.

rawEventDetails: Speaker Joseph Devietti Affiliation University of Pennsylvania Details Event Description Abstract: Modern processor architectures are complex machines due to decades' worth of performance optimizations. This complexity can lead to subtle performance issues at the microarchitectural level that are very difficult to diagnose and repair. Fortunately, modern processors also contain a rich set of performance monitoring facilities that enable introspection of many aspects of program execution. I will share our work on techniques to diagnose and repair, in running programs, two particular performance issues: adjusting code layout on-the-fly to match current hot code paths, and adding data prefetch instructions on-the-fly to improve current data access patterns. I will also discuss some research side quests in bringing GPU acceleration to neurosymbolic programs (which combine deep learning with symbolic reasoning to achieve better data efficiency, interpretability, and generalizability compared to standalone deep learning approaches), and chip design tools that are more idiot-/AI-friendly. Bio: Joseph Devietti is an Associate Professor in the Department of Computer & Information Science at the University of Pennsylvania. His research focuses on making parallel computers easier to program, leveraging techniques across the computing stack, including computer architecture, compilers, runtime systems and programming languages. He was awarded an Intel Early Career Faculty Honor in 2013, and had a paper selected as one of the Top Picks from 2022 Computer Architecture Conferences. He earned his PhD in Computer Science & Engineering from the University of Washington in 2012. Sponsor Emerging Frontiers in Computer Architecture and Systems

title: Generative Biology - Learning to Program Cellular Machines and Systems
speaker: Wendell Lim
content: Living cells are capable of sensing their environment, integrating this information, and making complex decisions. These decisions are, at their heart, mediated by genetically encoded molecular circuits. In the field of synthetic biology, we have been engineering modular molecular components capable of sensing and actuating and using these components to create diverse cell-based biological programs. These include programming immune cells to search the body for combinatorial molecular signatures of disease (e.g., cancer, autoimmunity, and degeneration). We are also programming multicellular
rawEventDetails: Speaker Wendell Lim Affiliation University of California San Francisco Details Event Description Living cells are capable of sensing their environment, integrating this information, and making complex decisions. These decisions are, at their heart, mediated by genetically encoded molecular circuits. In the field of synthetic biology, we have been engineering modular molecular components capable of sensing and actuating and using these components to create diverse cell-based biological programs. These include programming immune cells to search the body for combinatorial molecular signatures of disease (e.g., cancer, autoimmunity, and degeneration). We are also programming multicellular systems to understand the principles that drive multi-cellular self-organization, such as the development of tissues and organs. These synthetic biology tools and approaches are helping to define the fundamental logic underlying complex biological behaviors and provide new avenues to create useful synthetic cellular devices and living materials. rawEventDetails: Speaker Mohamed Abdelfattah Affiliation Cornell Tech Details Event Description Abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference is computationally expensive and increasingly dominated by memory bandwidth. This talk presents a set of hardware, software, and algorithmic techniques that address these bottlenecks through cross-layer co-design, spanning numerical representation, tensor compression, and custom hardware accelerator architectures. I make the case that we are well past the point of "traditional codesign" to get to higher computing speeds, and we need to move towards Extreme Codesign where the lines between algorithm, software, and hardware abstractions are being blurred in the pursuit of performance for AI systems. Bio: Mohamed Abdelfattah is an Assistant Professor at Cornell Tech and in the Electrical and Computer Engineering Department at Cornell University. His research group is designing the next generation of machine-learning-centric computer systems for both datacenters and mobile devices. He received his BSc from the German University in Cairo, his MSc from the University of Stuttgart, and his PhD from the University of Toronto. After his PhD, Mohamed spent six years at Intel and Samsung Research. Recently, he co-founded a startup, Makora, to automate performance optimizations for AI. He is the recipient of multiple best paper awards, the Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarship, and the NSF CAREER award. Sponsor Emerging Frontiers in Computer Architecture and Systems

title: Crystal Engineering in the Pharmaceutical Industry: Opportunities for Further Innovation
content: Crystal engineering has been used within the pharmaceutical industry for multiple decades, primarily applied to batch processes. Crystal engineering is employed for the control of crystal attributes such as crystal form, particle size, particle morphology as well as impurity rejection. rawEventDetails: Speaker Christopher Burcham Affiliation University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Details Event Description Crystal engineering has been used within the pharmaceutical industry for multiple decades, primarily applied to batch processes. Crystal engineering is employed for the control of crystal attributes such as crystal form, particle size, particle morphology as well as impurity rejection. While applied across intermediate steps, crystal engineering is often utilized for the isolation of the active pharmaceutical ingredient, as these particle attributes can directly impact the bioavailability of the drug when used in solid oral dosage forms. Concurrent with the increased utilization of particle engineering techniques, the pharmaceutical industry has also rediscovered continuous processing and as a natural result there has been an increased interest in continuous crystallization and isolation of pharmaceutical intermediates and APIs. Continuous crystallization presents unique challenges to the control of physical properties of active pharmaceutical ingredients by direct crystallization when compared to batch crystallization processes. These limitations can be overcome to some extent by the implementation of in-situ milling and other process intensification technologies. Development of these processes has historically been experiential through trial-and-error experimentation – which leads to long development cycles, and the need for significant quantities of materials to fund the development studies. Application and utilization of population balance models (PBM) significantly decrease both the development cycle time and the material needs – a case study demonstrating the efficiency gains of using PBMs will be presented. While the utilization of PBMs greatly decreases the development timeframe, the overall process development cycle is quite linear, such that the development of the process cannot begin until many other activities are completed, all of which rely on the selection of the crystal form that will be carried forward – which until recently has been done through extensive crystal screening studies. Innovations in ab-initio crystal structure predictions (CSP) offer the promise of transforming polymorph screening and selection by predicting all possible polymorphs of a given organic molecule along with the associated free energies of each predicted form. These advances in the ability to predict crystal form as well as crystal growth have progressed to such a point where one can ask – can the linear process development workflow be replaced through in-silico simulations? (Burcham et al, 2024). An in-silico workflow for the digital design of crystallization processes starting from the chemical structure of the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) through to process development will be presented. The opportunities, current limitations and prospects for future innovation of this approach will be discussed. 1. Burcham, C. L., et al. (2024). "PharmaceuScal Digital Design: From Chemical Structure through Crystal Polymorph to Conceptual Crystallization Process." Crystal Growth & Design 24(13): 5417–5438.

title: Synthetic Data, Real Benefits: Reliable Inference and Principled Model Steering
content: AbstractAI models are powerful, yet their use in practice raises two fundamental challenges. The first is trust: how can we make reliable inferences from black-box models when we only have a few reference examples to rely on? The second is steerability: how can we guide AI generation when we can recognize the outputs we prefer but cannot precisely quantify our preferences? In this talk, I will show how statistics and AI can empower one another to tackle both challenges.The first part focuses on reliable inference under limited data. I'll introduce
rawEventDetails: Speaker Yaniv Romano Affiliation Technion- Israel Institute of Technology Details Event Description Abstract AI models are powerful, yet their use in practice raises two fundamental challenges. The first is trust: how can we make reliable inferences from black-box models when we only have a few reference examples to rely on? The second is steerability: how can we guide AI generation when we can recognize the outputs we prefer but cannot precisely quantify our preferences? In this talk, I will show how statistics and AI can empower one another to tackle both challenges. The first part focuses on reliable inference under limited data. I'll introduce General Synthetic-Powered Inference (GESPI), a framework that safely enhances the sample efficiency of any statistical inference procedure—such as conformal prediction and hypothesis testing—by adaptively leveraging synthetic data. GESPI provides distribution-free error control regardless of synthetic-data quality while improving utility when those data are informative. I'll demonstrate its applicability across domains ranging from predictive uncertainty quantification to principled win-rate evaluation of large reasoning models. I'll also discuss how these ideas can support large-scale scientific discovery with false discovery rate control. In the second part, I'll introduce Preference-based Metropolis-Hastings (Pref-MH): a model-steering framework that leverages pairwise votes from an LLM judge to generate data satisfying complex properties of interest. Pref-MH exploits a novel connection between MH and the Bradley-Terry preference model. This connection enables rigorous steering of a base AI generator toward a target distribution that favors outputs preferred by the judge, without ever needing to estimate the judge's latent reward. Finally, I'll demonstrate Pref-MH in molecular design and show how the resulting synthetic data improve downstream inference when incorporated into GESPI. Bio Yaniv Romano is an associate professor in the Departments of Electrical and Computer Engineering and Computer Science at the Technion. He is also affiliated with NVIDIA as a visiting professor. Previously, he was a postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Statistics at Stanford University. Yaniv holds a PhD, an MSc, and a BSc in electrical engineering, all from the Technion. His super-resolution technology, invented with Peyman Milanfar, has been integrated into Google’s flagship products, including Pixel phones. His uncertainty quantification method, developed with Emmanuel Candès, was used by The Washington Post to estimate outstanding votes during the U.S. presidential election. Yaniv has received several honors and awards, including an ERC Starting Grant, the SIAG/IS Early Career Prize, the Sheila Samson Prime Minister’s Prize (Researcher Recruitment Prize), the IEEE Signal Processing Society Best Paper Award, the Alon Scholarship, the Krill Prize for Excellence in Scientific Research, and the Henry Taub Prize for Academic Excellence. speaker: Dr. Rebecca Ciez, Purdue University
content: Abstract: Electrifying energy-intensive industries is a key component of reducing fossil fuel consumption and meeting decarbonization goals, but these end uses have been slower to transition than other sectors of the economy because of the diversity of industrial processes, the heat and temperature requirements involved, and the capital-intensive nature of existing infrastructure. The scale of transitioning this sector of the economy will also have significant impacts on the broader electricity sector, including changes in demand patterns, grid capacity requirements, and
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Electrifying energy-intensive industries is a key component of reducing fossil fuel consumption and meeting decarbonization goals, but these end uses have been slower to transition than other sectors of the economy because of the diversity of industrial processes, the heat and temperature requirements involved, and the capital-intensive nature of existing infrastructure. The scale of transitioning this sector of the economy will also have significant impacts on the broader electricity sector, including changes in demand patterns, grid capacity requirements, and infrastructure investment needs, all of which need to be taken into account in order to evaluate the impact of industrial technologies. This seminar will introduce multiscale modeling frameworks used to analyze the impact of industrial electrification on the broader electricity system, from individual process-level changes up to system-wide effects, as well as the lifecycle analysis methods used to assess the environmental impacts of these electrified alternatives across their full value chain. In addition to the environmental impacts of industrial electrification, these methods also consider the impacts on energy prices and the cost of producing goods via electrified alternatives, offering a more complete picture of the economic trade-offs involved in this transition. Examples of industrial electrification pathways at different scales will be presented, including individual facilities with small and large energy demand, as well as broader scenarios considering the electrification of entire industrial sectors like the steel industry, illustrating how these modeling approaches can inform decision-making at both the facility and sector level. Bio: Dr. Rebecca Ciez is an Assistant Professor in Mechanical Engineering and Sustainability Engineering and Environmental Engineering at Purdue University. Prior to Purdue, she was a postdoctoral researcher at the Andlinger Center for Energy and the Environment. Her research combines methods from engineering, quantitative policy analysis, and economics to consider the economic and environmental impacts of energy systems and technologies. Her research group uses these methods to consider both electrochemical energy storage technologies and industrial electrification technologies. Dr. Ciez was a Negative Emissions Science Scialog Fellow, and was named a 40 under 40 rising star in Environmental Engineering and Science by the American Academy of Environmental Engineers & Scientists. Dr. Ciez’s work has been published in journals including ACS Energy Letters, Energy and Environmental Science, Joule, and Nature Sustainability. She holds a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering from Columbia University and a Ph.D. in Engineering and Public Policy from Carnegie Mellon University. Event Category MAE Departmental Seminars

title: Flow, Structure, and Motion Correlation in Nearly-jammed Suspensions
content: Some general introductory ideas about suspensions of particles in liquids as well as a set of new findings will be developed in this talk. Suspensions are found in many forms and settings, and the compositions and properties can vary widely. However, certain issues prevail: one is the influence of the liquid through hydrodynamic interactions, and a second is the importance of the solid fraction and interparticle forces in controlling the flow properties, which we usually call the rheology of the material. Suspensions include colloidal dispersions of nanoparticles as well as cases
rawEventDetails: Speaker Jeffrey Morris Affiliation The City College of New York Details Event Description Some general introductory ideas about suspensions of particles in liquids as well as a set of new findings will be developed in this talk. Suspensions are found in many forms and settings, and the compositions and properties can vary widely. However, certain issues prevail: one is the influence of the liquid through hydrodynamic interactions, and a second is the importance of the solid fraction and interparticle forces in controlling the flow properties, which we usually call the rheology of the material. Suspensions include colloidal dispersions of nanoparticles as well as cases involving somewhat larger particles such as cement, ceramics, and mud. The last three are all examples of dense suspensions, with solid fraction approaching the limit of flowability known as jamming. Because the rheology most often depends on the magnitude of the applied forces (e.g. pressure gradient in a pipe flow), suspensions are complex fluids – or they may be unyielded soft solids that can be caused to flow by enough force, as seen in the examples of cement mortars or muds. Here, we will present results based on simulations of suspensions approaching jamming to illustrate the unique features of these materials. These include discontinuous shear thickening (DST) as well as shear-induced jamming. The role of interparticle forces, including conservative and frictional contact forces, and the imposed stress in this process will be briefly reviewed, followed by our current examination of structures that are found to be related to the abrupt flow transitions. On approach to jamming, these structures develop as a result of the progressive reduction of the particle degrees of freedom in their motion as networks of contacts are formed. These networks rapidly break and reform during flow, but give rise to strongly correlated near-rigid motions of identifiable domains or “transient clusters.” The resulting fluctuations in motion become dominant as jamming is approached. In the DST regime, the contact number is found to fluctuate very strongly, but can result in highly connected but once again transient structures; system-spanning, or percolating, structures of frictionally-contacting particles are found to have important influence on the observed rheology.

title: Peculiarities of Heat-Driven and Light-Driven Evaporation
content: Joint CEE/MAE Distinguished SeminarAbstract:This talk will discuss two peculiar effects we recently discovered: the photomolecular effect and the evaporative refrigeration effect. To explain super-thermal solar-interfacial evaporation from hydrogels and other porous materials, we hypothesize that photons can directly cleave off water clusters at the liquid-vapor interface in a way similar to the photoelectric effect, which we call the photomolecular effect. I will discuss experimental evidence we have so far. This photomolecular
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Joint CEE/MAE Distinguished Seminar Abstract: This talk will discuss two peculiar effects we recently discovered: the photomolecular effect and the evaporative refrigeration effect. To explain super-thermal solar-interfacial evaporation from hydrogels and other porous materials, we hypothesize that photons can directly cleave off water clusters at the liquid-vapor interface in a way similar to the photoelectric effect, which we call the photomolecular effect. I will discuss experimental evidence we have so far. This photomolecular evaporation process may exist widely in nature. Our studies on photomolecular evaporation also led us to investigate peculiarities in thermal evaporation. At an evaporating interface, a temperature discontinuity exists between the liquid and the vapor sides, which was predicted by theories and observed in some experiments. However, the existing theories cannot explain experiments. We develop a new interfacial condition that can be used to couple transport on both sides of the interface, leading to agreements between theory and experiments. Our modeling reveals the existence of a new refrigeration effect: the vapor temperature can drop below that of the liquid film and in fact, lower than even the condensing surface temperature. This effect has yet to be confirmed experimentally and may find applications in air-conditioning and refrigeration. title: Selective Ion Transport in Hydration-limited Sub-nm Pores of Polymer Membranes
content: Ion transport under nanoscale confinement and in the presence of charge is poorly understood from a fundamental perspective. Under the conditions of dielectric saturation that arise in nanoscale pores, the classical ideas that guide our understanding of electrostatic interactions break down, and new principles that account for the role of pore geometry and chemistry on water structure and ion interactions are needed. At the same time, our ability to develop such principles is hindered by the challenge of generating relevant well-defined geometries that enable experimental studies over
rawEventDetails: Speaker Chinedum Osuji Affiliation University of Pennsylvania Details Event Description Ion transport under nanoscale confinement and in the presence of charge is poorly understood from a fundamental perspective. Under the conditions of dielectric saturation that arise in nanoscale pores, the classical ideas that guide our understanding of electrostatic interactions break down, and new principles that account for the role of pore geometry and chemistry on water structure and ion interactions are needed. At the same time, our ability to develop such principles is hindered by the challenge of generating relevant well-defined geometries that enable experimental studies over statistically meaningful volumes such that experimental data can be more confidently considered alongside data from computational efforts. Beyond the fundamental implications, new understanding is needed to drive the rational design of materials for ion separations in critical minerals production and resource recovery, among other examples, where the need to distinguish between ions of the same valency and charge imposes a severe challenge. Here, we examine transport of ions in polymer membranes with well-defined sub-1 nm pores. The membranes are charged, modestly hydrated nanoporous polymers produced by crosslinking self-assembled lyotropic mesophases with direct hexagonal and gyroid nanostructures. This work addresses the roles of hydration, pore geometry and ion identity on transport using a combination of electrochemical and NMR measurements, and molecular simulation. Our results highlight the roles of hydration, solubility, pore size, and ion-pore wall interactions in dictating transport in the pores. They provide new insight regarding transport under nanoscale confinement in the presence of charge and that we suggest could be relevant for the development of materials for challenging ion separations.

title: Internet of Radar Things: Turning a World of Radios into One Radar
content: Abstract: Almost every wireless device transmits over the air to communicate, and an increasing fraction of these devices can also use their signals to sense the physical world. As integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is moving from research into standards, these radios periodically sense the world from the response of the environment on their transmitted signal. At the same time, WiFi, cellular, and automotive platforms are expanding into millimeter-wave spectrum, where wide bandwidths and compact antenna arrays provide fine spatial and temporal
rawEventDetails: Speaker Akshay Gadre Affiliation University of Washington Details Event Description Abstract: Almost every wireless device transmits over the air to communicate, and an increasing fraction of these devices can also use their signals to sense the physical world. As integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is moving from research into standards, these radios periodically sense the world from the response of the environment on their transmitted signal. At the same time, WiFi, cellular, and automotive platforms are expanding into millimeter-wave spectrum, where wide bandwidths and compact antenna arrays provide fine spatial and temporal resolution, Together, these trends create the foundation for an Internet of Radar Things (IoRT) : a dense population of access points, base stations, vehicles, robots, and mobile devices whose radios can sense while they communicate. Unfortunately, a network of these sensing-capable radios operates largely as n isolated monostatic sensors: each independently occupies spectrum, illuminates an overlapping environment, and retains only the echoes at its own small aperture. These discarded paths contain complementary viewpoints that could extend coverage through occlusions, distinguish physical objects from multipath ghosts, and synthesize apertures far larger than any individual device. This talk presents a unique vision to coordinate these distributed radars coherently to turn this world of radios into one mega-radar. In this talk, we will first present the unique capabilities such a coherent future could enable and how we achieve coherence on commodity off-the-shelf radars to demonstrate these solutions. We specifically show how distributed radars can eliminate ghost artifacts and improve sensing capability, how we can extract material characteristics of objects using this large aperture and how we can use coherence-in-motion to develop free-flowing hand-held imaging solutions for mmWave radars. We further demonstrate how these improvements can directly translate to WiFi and cellular radios. Finally, we end the talk by describing open challenges that still need to be addressed to unleash the true potential of the Internet of Radar Things. Bio: Akshay Gadre is an Assistant Professor at Electrical and Computer Engineering department at the University of Washington. He leads the Networking and Emerging Wireless Technologies (NEWT) Lab at the University of Washington where they explore the upcoming application domains such as satellite IoT, mmWave radars and underwater devices, to apply wireless expertise for improving communication and sensing capability of these devices while preserving the security and privacy of sensor data. Further, the lab explores novel interaction mechanisms for future smart devices such as smart gloves and XR systems using novel force sensing and gaze modalities. His previous research at Carnegie Mellon University operated at the intersection of wireless, mobile and cyber-physical systems with special focus on empowering the low-power Internet-of-Things devices deployed on earth and space. NEWT Lab is also translating these technologies to industry partners including General Motors and IDD Aerospace. His work is published in premier wireless and mobile systems venues including ACM MobiCom, MobiSys, SenSys, Transactions on Sensor Networks and NSDI. Their lab's work has won two best paper awards, four best demo awards, two best-demo runner up awards at these venues. Both Akshay and his students have received the best PhD Forum presentation award at the CPS-IoT Week. Their work has been recognized with the T-Mobile T-Challenge 2024 Most Engaging Presentation Award for their vision of radio digital twins for consumer applications as well as the AFRL SDR University Challenge Best Demo award for developing a cheap SDR platform for exploring satellite networking. He has been also recognized with the ACM SIGBED-SIGSOFT Frank Anger Memorial Award 2021 for his cross-disciplinary work on IoT networking, cyber-security and software engineering. He was also recognized as a Distinguished TPC Member for his services to ACM SenSys 2026. He received his Bachelor of Technology (Honors) and Master of Technology degrees in Computer Science and Engineering from IIT Madras as well as a Ph.D in Electrical and Computer Engineering from Carnegie Mellon University. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: The exploration of primitive bodies in the solar system, such as asteroids and comets, is driven by scientific questions about the early solar system, long-term goals of utilizing primitive body resources in space, and the protection of the planet from hazardous impacts. Motivated by these concerns, there have been many missions to these small bodies over the last few decades, with each one uncovering new details about these bodies that further motivate their exploration, while identifying new technologies that are needed to continue our progress. Despite past success, there still remain significant challenges across a range of scientific and technical issues associated with small body exploration. Several recent missions have opened up new possibilities for their exploration, and some current and planned missions will continue our progress in the exploration and characterization of these bodies. These missions, both from NASA and from international agencies, are pushing boundaries by exploring new classes of asteroids and improving our ability to interact with them. This talk will introduce the motivations for exploring these primitive bodies, discuss recent progress made by a range of missions, and outline their future exploration, identifying what new questions can and are being pursued. Before this, he held faculty positions at the University of Michigan and Iowa State, and was a senior member of the technical staff at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Scheeres is a member of the National Academy of Engineering and the International Academy of Astronautics, an Honorary Fellow of the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, and a Fellow of the American Astronautical Society. Asteroid 8887 is named “Scheeres” to recognize his contributions to the scientific understanding of the dynamical environment about asteroids. Event Category MAE Departmental Seminars

content: Meeting the growing demand for energy requires the development of innovative energy conversion and storage processes beyond conventional thermal technologies and electrocatalysis plays a central role in this transition. While electrocatalysis shares a number of common design principles with thermal catalysis, they also differ greatly. In addition, electrochemical processes often occur at liquid-solid interface under potential, posting new challenges in
rawEventDetails: Speaker Hong Yang Affiliation University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Details Event Description Meeting the growing demand for energy requires the development of innovative energy conversion and storage processes beyond conventional thermal technologies and electrocatalysis plays a central role in this transition. While electrocatalysis shares a number of common design principles with thermal catalysis, they also differ greatly. Besides reactivity and selectivity, durability and stability under electrochemical reaction conditions are required for an electrocatalyst. In addition, electrochemical processes often occur at liquid-solid interface under potential, posting new challenges in design. In this presentation, I will discuss our research effort, aiming at uncovering structural design for electrocatalysts. Specifically, I will present the studies on structural and interfacial control of metal oxide and alloy electrocatalysts for oxygen evolution reaction (OER) which occurs in a range of chemical processes, such as hydrogen production from water splitting. Our finding suggests defect engineering is often central in the design of high-performance electrocatalysts for site and crystalline phase tunable complex oxides (i.e., rutile, pyrochlore, and perovskite) and for strained alloys. Flexibility in lattice of complex oxides (A x B y O z ) and tunability of surface strain of alloys often provide the controls of surface and lattice structures that affect the electrocatalytic reaction pathways and performance. Notably, unlike thermal catalysts, proper design of structural defects could simultaneously enhance both activity and stability of electrocatalysts. Valence band analysis, in situ Raman spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, molecular probe and isotope kinetic studies, together with electrochemical characterizations, have been used to identify reactive intermediates and to understand reaction mechanisms.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Thermal conductivity is a basic and familiar property of materials: silver spoons conduct heat well and plastic does not. High thermal conductivity is desirable for heat exchangers and thermal management while low thermal conductivity is needed for thermal insulation. In recent years, the combined efforts of materials scientists, engineers, physicists, and chemists have succeeded in pushing-back long-established limits in the thermal conductivity of materials. Advances in experimental methods have expanded the range of materials that can be studied with high throughput and high accuracy. Theory and computation are playing an increasingly importantrole in guiding and interpreting experiments. In this lecture, I will highlight recent discoveries of extremes of thermal conductivity of materials using examples from hard and soft matter (cubic boron arsenide, ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene, disordered layered 2D materials, functionalized fullerenes) and our work on expanding the upper and lower limits of the thermal conductivity ofcommon polymers (polyurethanes, epoxies, polyesters, and polyimides). Bio: Dr. David Cahill is the Grainger Distinguished Chair in Engineering, and Professor of Materials Science and Engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. He served as department head from 2010 to 2018. His research program advances physical insights on thermal transport at the nanoscale; extremes of low and high thermal conductivity in polymers; thermal metrology for microelectronics;the thermal science of electrochemical cells and battery materials; and materials for quantum computing. Cahill received the 2018 Innovation in Materials Characterization Award of the Materials Research Society, the 2015 Touloukian Award of the American Society of Mechanical Engineers, and the Klemens Award from the International Conference on Phonon Scattering in Condensed Matter. He is a fellow of the MRS, the American Physical Society, the AAAS, and is an elected member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. Event Category MAE Departmental Seminars

title: Nuclear Electric Propulsion: Progress, Challenges, and the Path to High-Power Space Systems
speaker: Dr. Kurt Polzin, NASA
content: Abstract:Nuclear electric propulsion (NEP) offers the potential to fundamentally expand the capability and reach of spacecraft, but realizing that potential requires overcoming significant challenges in reactor technology, power conversion and distribution, thermal management, electric propulsion, and system integration. This seminar will examine the current state of NEP development, highlighting recent progress while exploring the demanding requirements associated with operating high-power systems continuously for years or even decades in the space environment.
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Nuclear electric propulsion (NEP) offers the potential to fundamentally expand the capability and reach of spacecraft, but realizing that potential requires overcoming significant challenges in reactor technology, power conversion and distribution, thermal management, electric propulsion, and system integration. This seminar will examine the current state of NEP development, highlighting recent progress while exploring the demanding requirements associated with operating high-power systems continuously for years or even decades in the space environment. Particular attention will be given to high-power electric propulsion, lightweight high-temperature radiators, radiation-tolerant power electronics, and the testing and evaluation infrastructure needed to mature these technologies and demonstrate integrated systems. The discussion will also consider an evolutionary path toward increasingly capable NEP systems, beginning with lower-power long-duration missions and building toward higher-power systems for human exploration and deep-space science. Finally, the seminar will examine the technology investments and national test and evaluation capabilities needed to turn this vision into a sustained spaceflight capability. BIO : Dr. Kurt Polzin is a senior aerospace engineer and internationally recognized expert in advanced space propulsion. He is from the George C. Marshall Space Flight Center and currently serves as NASA’s Capability Manager for Advanced Propulsion within the Space Transportation Program, where he leads technology development activities spanning electric propulsion, green propellants, solar sails, and other advanced propulsion technologies. Previously, he served as Chief Engineer for NASA’s Space Nuclear Propulsion portfolio as the engineering technical authority for a national, multi-agency effort to advance nuclear thermal and nuclear electric propulsion systems. Dr. Polzin has authored more than 150 technical publications and has conducted research and development in electric propulsion, plasma physics, nuclear propulsion, spacecraft power systems, and advanced space transportation. He is an AIAA Fellow and recipient of the AIAA Engineer of the Year and Plasmadynamics & Lasers Awards. Dr. Polzin received his B.S. in Aerospace Engineering from The Ohio State University and his M.A. and Ph.D. in Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering from Princeton University. rawEventDetails: Speaker Danielle Mai Affiliation Stanford University Details Event Description Evolution allows organisms to adapt to their environments, yet some molecular patterns stay constant through billions of years of evolution. These patterns encode the secrets of biological materials, such that similar patterns often emerge in different materials with similar functions. For example, a family of elastin proteins form stretchable fibers, which allow the constant movement of human skin, blood vessels, and lungs. We aim to decode the secrets of biological materials by investigating sequence patterns in repetitive proteins, towards establishing systematic protein sequence–biomaterial property relationships. This talk explores two classes of repetitive proteins as stimuli-responsive biopolymers. First, we investigate bacterial proteins that undergo conformational changes in response to calcium ions. We modify hydrophobicity, electrostatics, and sequence heterogeneity to demonstrate sequence-dependent, reversible folding and domain size changes in response to calcium ions. We also identify structural features that give rise to ion selectivity, which is not yet well-predicted by AI/ML tools. Second, we introduce enzymatic stimuli to drive isothermal phase separation of elastin-like polypeptides (ELPs). ELPs have drawn interest as heat-responsive biopolymers, such that ELPs undergo reversible phase separation from water upon heating. However, temperature is not always a convenient trigger, especially in biological environments that maintain near-constant temperature, pH, and ionic composition. To expand ELP function, we program a mechanism for isothermal phase separation upon proteolytic cleavage of a di-block ELP. This mechanism presents a new opportunity to exploit biological triggers for ELP phase behavior and self-assembly processes. Overall, we demonstrate repetitive proteins as tunable and modular building blocks for functional biomaterials.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: In robotics, we have spent a lot of time building really good maps from noisy sensor data. Who doesn’t like a nice, crisp, globally consistent map? Over the last 20 years, I have been exploring a paradigm to robot navigation that eschews such globally consistent maps in favour of graphs of local maps, which are cheaper to construct, store, and query. These topometric maps enable so-called teach-and-repeat (T&R) navigation. In this talk, I will give a progress update on some of the new things we are doing with T&R including using different primary sensors, teaching with one robot and repeating with another, repeating with multiple robots together, and enabling end-user applications such as Arctic patrol and lunar cargo transport. Hopefully I will convince you that local maps are all you need (i.e.,sufficient) for a lot of common robotics scenarios. I will also try to convince you that local maps are necessary! Bio: Timothy Barfoot (University of Toronto Institute for Aerospace Studies – UTIAS) works in the area of autonomy for mobile robots targeting a variety of applications. He develops methods (localization, mapping, planning, control) to allow robots to operate over long periods of time in large-scale, unstructured, three-dimensional environments, using rich onboard sensing (e.g., cameras, laser rangefinders, radar) and computation. Timothy holds a BASc (9T6+PEY, Aerospace Option) from the UofT Engineering Science program and a PhD from UTIAS in robotics. He took up his academic position at UTIAS in May 2007, after spending four years at MDA Space (builder of the well-known Canadarm space manipulators), where he developed autonomous vehicle navigation technologies for both planetary rovers and terrestrial applications such as underground mining. He is a Fellow of the IEEE, a Fellow of the Canadian Academy of Engineering, held a Canada Research Chair for the full 10 years, was an Early Researcher Awardee in the Province of Ontario, and has received three paper awards at the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2010, 2021, 2025) as well as four at the Conference on Robots and Vision (CRV 2014, 2016, 2023, 2025). Timothy began serving as Director (Dept. Head) of UTIAS on 1 July 2026, and previously served as Director of the UofT Robotics Institute,Director of the UofT Collaborative Specialization in Robotics, co-Faculty Advisor of UofT's self-driving car team that won the SAE Autodrivecompetition several times, Chair of the UofT Engineering Science Robotics Major, and was a Faculty Affiliate of the Vector Institute. He wasa Visiting Professor at the University of Oxford (2013, 2024) and worked as Director of Autonomous Systems at Apple in California (2017-9).He holds the position of Distinguished Engineer at Oxa Autonomy Ltd (parttime). He is the Editor in Chief of the IEEE Transactions on Field Robotics (T-FR), deputy EiC of the International Journal of Robotics Research (IJRR), served on the Foundation Board of Robotics: Scienceand Systems (RSS), and served as the General Chair of Field and Service Robotics (FSR) 2015, which was held in Toronto. He is the author of State Estimation for Robotics (Cambridge 2017, 2024), which is free to download from his webpage, and co-editor/co-author of the SLAM Handbook (Cambridge 2026). Event Category MAE Departmental Seminars

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description How is it possible that 1/4 of the Nobel Prizes in Physics since 2006 have been for astrophysics? All 5 of them came from new technologies, and two required space observatories. I’ll review the breakthrough ideas that grew into discoveries, and suggest where future technologies might go.The JWST is working brilliantly, and has found Little Red Dots, the current mystery object. But there’s still no Earth 2.0. The DKIST solar telescope with adaptive optics is working beautifully. The Vera Rubin Telescope is online, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will be launched just before this colloquium to study dark matter, dark energy, and exoplanets, and the 39 m diameter Extremely Large Telescope will be doing science around 2030. Among the new possibilities: the Habitable Worlds Observatory, a workhorse UV-near IR observatory with a coronagraph for exoplanets, and X-ray and far IR observatories from Probe class ($1B) to flagships. New detector and mirror technologies are making both exciting. The NAUTILUS concept will use molded glass lenses up to 8 m in diameter in space to collect light for spectroscopy. We’re also developing hybrid observatories combining telescopes and interferometers on the ground with satellites. The Landolt absolute photometric calibrator beacon will fly in 2029, and the CELESTE mission is a proposed Small Explorer to offer a laser beacon for adaptive optics to the ELT, giving it diffraction-limited image quality at visible wavelengths where the sky is darkest. An orbiting starshade could cast a star shadow on the ELT and enable imaging of another Earth in one minute. The Black Hole Explorer would extend the Event Horizon Telescope with an orbiting antenna could measure the spin of a black hole. If you can imagine it, you can build it. Event Category MAE Departmental Seminars
summaryRaw: New Technology for New Astrophysics
